role_decode.summary: This team runs the GPU clusters that serve large-model inference at extreme scale. They are not paying for someone who 'knows Kubernetes' — they are paying for someone who can keep expensive GPU fleets busy, route inference requests reliably, and stop a $30k/hr cluster from sitting idle or falling over. Every technology in the JD (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, Kubernetes, Ray) is evidence of five underlying problems: inference cost, GPU utilization, orchestration at scale, distributed resilience, and observability.

expensive_problems.why_paid: Inference is the company's largest recurring compute bill; every efficiency point is millions saved.
expensive_problems.jd_evidence: "inference solutions using vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM"

expensive_problems.problem: Why does GPU memory become the bottleneck?
expensive_problems.why_paid: GPU memory limits batch size and model placement — the core constraint of serving economics.

expensive_problems.problem: Why do latency and throughput compete?
expensive_problems.why_paid: User-facing latency SLOs vs. cluster utilization is the daily tradeoff this team manages.
Cluster orchestration is the substrate; misconfiguration wastes fleets and causes outages.
expensive_problems.jd_evidence: "large-scale, container-based cluster management and orchestration systems"

expensive_problems.why_paid: Models no longer fit on one GPU; splitting them multiplies failure modes and coordination cost.
expensive_problems.jd_evidence: "large model inference, distributed and parallel systems"

expensive_problems.problem: Why is scheduling GPU workloads across a cluster difficult?
expensive_problems.why_paid: Bad scheduling strands GPU capacity — idle accelerators are pure burn.
Resilience at this scale is a hiring requirement, not a bonus; partial failure is the default state.
You cannot manage a fleet you cannot see; monitoring is listed as a qualifying experience.
expensive_problems.jd_evidence: "resource management, scheduling, request routing, monitoring, or orchestration"

hard_requirements: Understanding of large model inference and distributed/parallel systems
Hands-on infra experience: resource management, scheduling, routing, monitoring, or orchestration

gap_map.transfer: Automation/control-systems background: an orchestrator is a control loop (desired state vs. actual state) — same mental model as PLC control logic.
gap_map.credibility_risk: "Have you ever operated a cluster?" — must have run one, broken it, and healed it, even at home-lab scale.

gap_map.transfer: Cost-of-downtime thinking from industrial ops maps directly to cost-of-idle-GPU thinking.
gap_map.credibility_risk: "Walk me through what happens memory-wise when a request hits an LLM server" — needs measured, first-hand numbers.

gap_map.problem: Why does GPU memory become the bottleneck?
gap_map.transfer: Strong hardware intuition: memory hierarchies, bandwidth, and thermal limits are physical constraints — home turf.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Intuition without measurement reads as hand-waving; must show profiler output, not analogies.

gap_map.problem: Why do latency and throughput compete?
gap_map.transfer: Queueing intuition from production-line and equipment-throughput experience.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Must express it in inference terms: batch size, TTFT vs. tokens/sec, SLOs.

gap_map.problem: Why is vLLM faster than naive inference?
gap_map.transfer: Reverse-engineering complex equipment → reverse-engineering the vLLM scheduler is the same skill.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Interviewers on this team will probe continuous batching and PagedAttention specifics.

gap_map.transfer: STRONG: preventive maintenance, sensor monitoring, and fault isolation are observability — the mindset is already professional-grade, only the tools are new.
gap_map.credibility_risk: "Which metrics would you page on?" — needs hands-on Prometheus/Grafana + SLO definitions.

gap_map.problem: Why is scheduling GPU workloads across a cluster difficult?
gap_map.transfer: Resource allocation under physical constraints (power, capacity planning) from industrial settings.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Named in the JD's qualification sentence — likely an interview theme.

gap_map.transfer: Understanding of how failures propagate through coupled systems.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Depth question; acceptable to reason from fundamentals if the fundamentals are demonstrably solid.

gap_map.transfer: STRONG: real incident-style troubleshooting on physical systems; failure-mode thinking is native.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Must translate to software failure classes: partitions, timeouts, retry storms, partial failure.

gap_map.transfer: None direct, but it is the smallest gap on the list and unlocks everything else.
gap_map.credibility_risk: Table stakes — a fumbled Docker answer ends the interview.

positioning.narrative: I am not a career software engineer learning about machines — I am a machines engineer who has moved into the software that runs them. I spent years keeping industrial equipment alive: diagnosing faults under time pressure, reading failure propagation across electrical, mechanical, and control systems, and working where downtime has a dollar cost per minute. AI compute infrastructure is the same discipline with a different substrate: a GPU fleet is industrial equipment, utilization is throughput, an incident is an incident. I am building public, measured evidence — serving benchmarks, cluster failure drills, postmortems — to prove the software half meets the bar my hardware half already does.
do_not_claim: Professional AI infrastructure or model-serving experience
Formal SRE or large-scale incident-response ownership
talking_points: Control-loop framing: 'Kubernetes reconciliation is a control loop — I've spent years around control loops that move physical machinery.'
Cost framing: 'I think in cost-of-downtime and cost-of-idle-capacity because I've worked where both are measured in real money.'
Failure framing: 'I've done root-cause analysis on systems where the failing component lies to you — software observability is the same hunt with better instruments.'
Evidence framing: every claim in the resume links to a repo, a benchmark table, or a postmortem.
Honest gap framing: 'I haven't operated production GPU fleets — here is the home-lab fleet I built, broke, and measured instead.'

primary.question: Why does Docker exist — and how does a model get served from inside a container?

secondary: P10 — What happens when a request hits an AI application?
stretch: P5 — How do systems communicate over HTTP?

evidence.artifact: Repo: small open model (e.g., a 1–3B LLM) served behind a FastAPI endpoint in Docker, with a request-path architecture diagram
evidence.done_when: A curl from a second machine returns a completion; README traces the request end-to-end (client → HTTP → container → model → response) and explains every hop.

interview: Explain 'why containers' in 2 minutes without notes

primary.question: Why does GPU memory become the bottleneck for inference?

secondary: P12 — Why GPUs instead of CPUs?
P35 — Why does memory bandwidth matter?
stretch: P39 — Why does mixed precision speed up AI?

evidence.artifact: Benchmark: same model on CPU vs. GPU (rented spot instance is fine) — tokens/sec, memory footprint vs. context length, profiler screenshots
evidence.done_when: A table shows measured memory growth as context length increases, and the README explains where the memory goes (weights vs. KV cache vs. activations) from the measurements, not from a blog post.

interview: Explain the GPU memory budget of an LLM server in 2 minutes

primary.question: Why do latency and throughput compete in model serving?

secondary: P15 — Why does KV cache exist?
P16 — Why does batching improve throughput?

evidence.artifact: Benchmark: naive HF serving vs. vLLM under a load generator — TTFT and tokens/sec vs. concurrency, plotted
evidence.done_when: The latency/throughput curve is plotted from own measurements and the writeup states the batch-size tradeoff numerically ('at concurrency N, p95 TTFT degraded X% while throughput gained Y%').

interview: 1 system design: design a model-serving endpoint with a p95 latency SLO

primary.question: Why is vLLM faster than naive inference?

secondary: Reverse-engineer the vLLM scheduler: continuous batching + PagedAttention

evidence.artifact: Writeup + diagram: 'How vLLM schedules requests' — annotated walk through the actual scheduler code path, with a control-loop analogy section
evidence.done_when: The diagram matches the real code (file/function names cited); a reader could follow one request through admission, batching, and KV block allocation.

primary.question: Why does Kubernetes exist — and what is it actually doing when it 'heals' a workload?

secondary: P7 — How do companies deploy without breaking everything?
stretch: P33 — Why do microservices increase complexity?

evidence.artifact: Repo: k3s cluster (2–3 nodes, VMs fine) running the Week-1 model service; kill pods and a node under load; failure-mode table of what broke and how reconciliation recovered
evidence.done_when: The failure-mode table has ≥6 induced failures with observed behavior, recovery time, and the reconciliation mechanism responsible — written like an industrial FMEA.

interview: Explain the reconciliation loop as a control loop in 2 minutes

primary.question: Why does observability matter — and what would I page on for a model-serving fleet?

secondary: P26 — Why does tail latency matter?

evidence.artifact: Demo: Prometheus + Grafana on the cluster — GPU/latency/saturation dashboards, 3 defined SLOs, 2 alert rules, and a recorded walkthrough
evidence.done_when: An induced fault (memory pressure or pod kill) visibly fires the right alert; the README argues WHY these 3 SLOs and not others.

interview: 1 system design: observability for an inference fleet

primary.question: Why is scheduling GPU workloads across a cluster difficult?

secondary: P22 — Why do GPUs sit idle?
stretch: P20 — first pass at distributed inference concepts

evidence.artifact: Repo: two model services sharing constrained GPU/compute on the cluster — measure utilization under three scheduling/routing policies, benchmark the differences
evidence.done_when: A utilization-vs-policy table shows measured differences and the writeup explains which policy strands capacity and why — framed as a capacity-allocation problem.

interview: Explain why idle GPUs are the most expensive failure mode in 2 minutes

primary.question: Why do distributed systems fail — and can I run an incident like a professional?

secondary: P20 — Why is distributed inference difficult? (synthesis)
stretch: Mock interview loop against the whole portfolio

evidence.artifact: Capstone postmortem: inject a compound failure (node loss + retry storm) into the full stack, run it as a real incident — timeline, detection, mitigation, root cause, action items
evidence.done_when: The postmortem would pass review by a senior SRE: blameless, timestamped, with a 'what the monitoring missed' section; portfolio README links all 8 weeks of evidence.

interview: Explain any portfolio project cold, in 2 minutes each
